text.headline: Modern History (1707 – 1947)
text.text:
Spectrum’s Modern History covers the history of India from the decline of the Mughal Empire to Independence (1707 to 1947).

Reading notes, key leaders, and pivotal national movements.

text.headline: Death of Aurangzeb & Decline of Mughals
text.text:
The death of Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb at Ahmednagar marked the end of the centralized imperial era. Succession wars and the rise of autonomous regional kingdoms (Marathas, Nawabs of Bengal, Awadh, and Nizam of Hyderabad) created a political vacuum swiftly exploited by European mercantilist powers.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 3: (Expansion & Consolidation of British Power in India)

media.caption: Emperor Aurangzeb reading in his later years

text.headline: Battle of Plassey
text.text:
British forces under Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Bengal, following the betrayal of commander Mir Jafar. This decisive battle laid the territorial foundation of the British East India Company's rule in India, transforming it from a trading company into a dominant sovereign authority.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 4: (Rise of the British Power in Bengal)

media.caption: Robert Clive meeting Mir Jafar after Plassey (1757)

text.headline: Battle of Buxar & Diwani Rights
text.text:
The combined forces of Mir Qasim (Nawab of Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daula (Nawab of Awadh), and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II were decisively defeated by Hector Munro at Buxar. Through the subsequent Treaty of Allahabad (1765), Clive acquired the Diwani (fiscal administration and revenue collection rights) over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 4: (Dual Government in Bengal (1765–1772))

media.caption: Shah Alam II granting the Diwani of Bengal to Lord Clive (August 1765)

text.headline: The Regulating Act of 1773
text.text:
The British Parliament passed its first major statute to regulate the administration of the East India Company. Warren Hastings was appointed the first Governor-General of Bengal, subordinating Madras and Bombay presidencies, and establishing the Supreme Court of Judicature at Calcutta (1774).

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 26: (Constitutional Development under British Rule)

media.caption: Warren Hastings, 1st Governor-General of Bengal appointed under the Regulating Act of 1773.
media.credit: George Stubbs / National Portrait Gallery, London

text.headline: The Revolt of 1857 (First War of Independence)
text.text:
Triggered by sepoy resentment at Meerut over greased cartridges and underlying colonial grievances, the rebellion spread across Northern and Central India under the nominal leadership of Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar. The revolt ended the reign of the East India Company and led directly to Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 transferring power to the British Crown.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 7: (The Revolt of 1857)

media.caption: Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal Emperor (1857)

text.headline: Lord Canning
text.text:
First Viceroy of India after the Crown takeover via Queen Victoria's 1858 Proclamation. Abolished the Doctrine of Lapse. Enacted the Indian Penal Code 1860, Code of Criminal Procedure 1861, and Indian Councils Act 1861.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 8: Crown Rule & Administrative Changes

text.headline: Lord Lawrence
text.text:
Former Chief Commissioner of Punjab. Established High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras (1865). Followed the policy of 'Masterly Inactivity' toward Afghanistan.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 10: Foreign Policy & Frontier Administration

text.headline: Lord Mayo
text.text:
Initiated financial decentralization by granting provincial governments fixed annual sums for services. Conducted the first all-India population census (1872). Assassinated in Andaman Islands in 1872.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 10: Financial Decentralisation

text.headline: Mahatma Gandhi
text.text:
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was the preeminent leader of the Indian independence movement. Pioneer of Satyagraha (resistance through mass non-violent civil disobedience), he led transformative campaigns including the Champaran Satyagraha, Non-Cooperation Movement, Salt March, and Quit India Movement.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 15: Emergence of Gandhi & Non-Violent Mass Movements

media.caption: Life and Philosophy of Mahatma Gandhi

text.headline: Benjamin Disraeli
text.text:
Conservative British Prime Minister. Formulated imperialist foreign policy in Asia. Passed the Royal Titles Act 1876 proclaiming Queen Victoria Kaiser-i-Hind (Empress of India). Appointed Lord Lytton as Viceroy; presided over the devastating Great Famine of 1876–78 and Second Anglo-Afghan War.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 10: Administrative Policies and Famines

media.caption: Benjamin Disraeli, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

text.headline: Lord Lytton
text.text:
Ultra-conservative Viceroy who organized the extravagant Delhi Durbar in 1877 during the peak of the Great Famine. Passed the oppressive Vernacular Press Act 1878 and Arms Act 1878. Provoked the disastrous Second Afghan War.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 10: Lytton's Reactionary Policies

text.headline: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
text.text:
Barrister, politician, and the founder of Pakistan. Initially an ambassador of Hindu-Muslim unity through the Congress and the Lucknow Pact (1916), Jinnah later led the All-India Muslim League, advocating for constitutional safeguards (14 Points). By 1940, he championed the Lahore Resolution based on the Two-Nation Theory, culminating in the partition of British India in 1947, where he served as Pakistan's first Governor-General.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 18: Nationalist Upsurge & Muslim League Politics

text.headline: William E. Gladstone
text.text:
Liberal Prime Minister ('The Grand Old Man'). Opposed Disraeli's aggressive imperialism; appointed Lord Ripon as Viceroy to enact progressive administrative and municipal reforms. Supported the Ilbert Bill and local self-government in India.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 10: Ripon's Reforms & Liberal Imperialism

text.headline: Lord Ripon
text.text:
Beloved liberal Viceroy ('Father of Local Self-Government'). Repealed the Vernacular Press Act in 1882; passed the First Factory Act (1881) improving child labor conditions; appointed the Hunter Education Commission (1882); strongly backed the Ilbert Bill (1883) to allow Indian judges to try Europeans.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 10: Ripon the Reformer

text.headline: Lord Dufferin
text.text:
Viceroy during whose tenure the Indian National Congress was founded in Bombay (December 1885) under the initiative of A. O. Hume. Later ridiculed the Congress as representing only a 'microscopic minority'. Completed the Third Anglo-Burmese War (1885).

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 11: Foundation of the Indian National Congress

text.headline: Lord Salisbury
text.text:
Conservative Prime Minister during the early years of the Indian National Congress. Oversaw passage of the Indian Councils Act 1892, which modestly expanded Indian non-official participation in provincial and imperial legislative councils.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 11: Constitutional Development (1892)

text.headline: Jawaharlal Nehru
text.text:
Central leader of the Indian National Congress alongside Gandhi, architect of the modern Indian nation-state, and India's first Prime Minister (1947–1964). Authored the historic 1929 Lahore 'Purna Swaraj' resolution, championed democratic socialism, non-alignment, and scientific temper.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 19: Civil Disobedience Movement & Round Table Conferences

media.caption: Documentary on Jawaharlal Nehru and the Freedom Movement

text.headline: Lord Salisbury (Final Ministry)
text.text:
Conservative PM during severe Indian famines (1896–97 and 1899–1900) and the Bubonic Plague outbreak. Appointed the energetic imperialist Lord Curzon as Viceroy in 1899.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 10: Famines and Imperial Administration

text.headline: Subhash Chandra Bose
text.text:
Charismatic nationalist leader and former Congress President (Haripura 1938, Tripuri 1939). After ideological differences with Gandhi regarding armed resistance, he escaped India in 1941, formed the Forward Bloc, and subsequently revitalized the Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj) with the slogan 'Give me blood, and I will give you freedom!'.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 23: Nationalist Movement During World War II & INA

text.headline: Lord Curzon
text.text:
Ambitious and imperialist Viceroy. Partitioned the province of Bengal in 1905 to weaken Indian nationalism, triggering the historic Swadeshi Movement. Passed the Indian Universities Act 1904, Ancient Monuments Preservation Act 1904, and set up the Department of Commerce and Industry.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 12: Era of Militant Nationalism & Partition of Bengal

text.headline: Arthur Balfour
text.text:
Conservative PM. Endorsed Lord Curzon's controversial Partition of Bengal in October 1905, which galvanized the radical Swadeshi and Boycott movements across India.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 12: Partition of Bengal & Swadeshi Movement

text.headline: Lord Minto II
text.text:
Co-architect of the Morley-Minto Reforms (1909), which introduced separate electorates for Muslims. Encouraged the Shimla Deputation (1906) which resulted in the founding of the All-India Muslim League in Dhaka.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 13: Morley-Minto Reforms & Separate Electorates

text.headline: H. H. Asquith
text.text:
Liberal PM. Enacted the Morley-Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909), introducing separate electorates for Muslims. Arranged King George V's Delhi Durbar of 1911 that annulled the Partition of Bengal and transferred the capital to Delhi.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 13: Morley-Minto Reforms (1909)

text.headline: Lord Hardinge II
text.text:
Annulled the Partition of Bengal in the 1911 Delhi Durbar attended by King George V. Transferred the imperial capital from Calcutta to Delhi (1911). Survived a revolutionary bomb attack by Rash Behari Bose at Chandni Chowk (1912). Welcomed Mahatma Gandhi's return from South Africa (January 1915).

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 14: First World War & Nationalist Response

text.headline: Lord Chelmsford
text.text:
Formulated the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (Government of India Act 1919) instituting dyarchy. Enacted the repressive Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act (Rowlatt Act) 1919; oversaw the Jallianwala Bagh massacre at Amritsar. Gandhi launched the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movement during his tenure.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 15: Emergence of Gandhi & Non-Cooperation

text.headline: David Lloyd George
text.text:
Coalition Prime Minister during and after WWI. Passed the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (Government of India Act 1919) establishing provincial dyarchy. Faced intense Indian fury after the Rowlatt Act and General Dyer's Jallianwala Bagh massacre, triggering Gandhi's nationwide Non-Cooperation Movement.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 15: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms & Non-Cooperation

text.headline: Rowlatt Satyagraha
text.text:
Nationwide hartal and satyagraha organized by Mahatma Gandhi against the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919 (Rowlatt Act), which authorized preventive detention and imprisonment without trial. It marked Gandhi's transition to all-India mass nationalist leadership.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 15: Emergence of Gandhi & Non-Violent Mass Movements

media.caption: Public demonstration against the Rowlatt Act (April 1919)

text.headline: Test Rowlatt Satyagraha
text.text:
Nationwide strike called by Mahatma Gandhi against Rowlatt Act.

Book Note: Spectrum's Modern India

text.headline: Jallianwala Bagh Massacre
text.text:
British troops commanded by Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer opened fire on a peaceful crowd gathered at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar to celebrate Baisakhi and protest the arrest of leaders Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal under the Rowlatt Act. Hundreds were killed and thousands injured, triggering widespread national outrage and Rabindranath Tagore renouncing his knighthood.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 15: Jallianwala Bagh Massacre & Hunter Committee

media.caption: Archival Record: Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (13 April 1919)

text.headline: Lord Reading
text.text:
Handled the suspension of the Non-Cooperation Movement after the Chauri Chaura incident (1922). Witnessed the birth of the Swaraj Party (1923 by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru), the Kakori Train Action (1925), and communal riots.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 17: Emergence of Swarajists & Socialists

text.headline: Stanley Baldwin
text.text:
Conservative PM. Appointed the all-white Simon Commission (1927) without Indian representatives, leading to violent nationwide protests, the death of Lala Lajpat Rai, and the formulation of the Nehru Report (1928).

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 18: Simon Commission & Nehru Report

text.headline: Lord Irwin
text.text:
Faced the boycott of the Simon Commission (1928), the Nehru Report (1928), and the Lahore Congress declaration of Purna Swaraj (1929). Gandhi launched the historic Salt March to Dandi (1930) and Civil Disobedience. Concluded the Gandhi-Irwin Pact on 5 March 1931, suspending the movement in exchange for releasing political prisoners.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 19: Civil Disobedience & Gandhi-Irwin Pact

text.headline: Ramsay MacDonald
text.text:
Labour PM who convened the three Round Table Conferences in London (1930–1932) to negotiate Indian constitutional reforms. Issued the controversial Communal Award (August 1932) creating separate electorates for Depressed Classes, resolved through Gandhi and Ambedkar's Poona Pact.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 19: Round Table Conferences & Communal Award

text.headline: Lord Willingdon
text.text:
Adopted harsh police measures and ordinances to crush resumed Civil Disobedience. Presided over the Second and Third Round Table Conferences, the Communal Award (1932), Poona Pact, and the formulation and enactment of the landmark Government of India Act 1935.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 20: Government of India Act 1935

text.headline: Lord Linlithgow
text.text:
Longest-serving Viceroy of India. Conducted 1937 provincial elections under the 1935 Act. Unilaterally committed India to World War II in 1939 without consulting Indian ministries. Formulated the August Offer (1940); crushed the Quit India Movement in August 1942 with military force; oversaw the disastrous 1943 Bengal Famine.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 21: Nationalist Response to War & August Offer

text.headline: Neville Chamberlain
text.text:
Conservative PM at the outbreak of WWII (September 1939). Supported Viceroy Linlithgow's unilateral declaration dragging India into WWII without consulting elected provincial ministries, prompting the resignation of all Congress provincial ministries in protest.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 21: Nationalist Response to World War II

text.headline: Caxton Hall Assassination (Udham Singh)
text.text:
Revolutionary Sardar Udham Singh assassinated Michael O'Dwyer (the former Lieutenant Governor of Punjab who endorsed the Jallianwala Bagh massacre) at Caxton Hall in London. Udham Singh was subsequently tried and hanged at Pentonville Prison, becoming a prominent martyr of the revolutionary struggle.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 15: Jallianwala Bagh & Revolutionary Retaliation

media.caption: Sardar Udham Singh and the Caxton Hall Retaliation

text.headline: Winston Churchill
text.text:
Wartime Coalition PM and staunch opponent of Indian self-rule. Declared he had not become Prime Minister to 'preside over the liquidation of the British Empire'. Dispatched the Cripps Mission (1942); imprisoned the entire Congress leadership after Quit India (1942). Presided over the man-made Bengal Famine of 1943 resulting in 3 million deaths.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 22: Quit India Movement & Famine of 1943

text.headline: Bengal Famine of 1943
text.text:
Devastating famine in the Bengal province of British India during World War II, leading to the death of an estimated 2 to 3 million people from starvation and epidemic diseases. Exacerbated by British wartime procurement, denial policies, and Churchill's refusal to divert shipping relief, it remains one of the greatest colonial humanitarian catastrophes.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 23: War-Time Economy & Famines in British India

media.caption: Archival & Historical Analysis of the Bengal Famine

text.headline: Lord Wavell
text.text:
Convened the Shimla Conference (1945) to reconstitute the Executive Council (Wavell Plan). Received the Cabinet Mission (1946). Handled the Royal Indian Navy (RIN) Mutiny of 1946, the formation of the Interim Government under Nehru, and Direct Action Day riots.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 23: Post-War Deadlocks & Wavell Plan

text.headline: Clement Attlee
text.text:
Labour Prime Minister who granted Indian Independence. Dispatched the Cabinet Mission (1946). Made the historic announcement in the House of Commons on 20 February 1947 stating Britain would quit India by June 1948. Appointed Lord Mountbatten and steered the Indian Independence Act 1947 through Parliament.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 24: Post-War Surge & Road to Independence

text.headline: Lord Mountbatten
text.text:
Last Viceroy of British India. Formulated the June 3rd Plan (Mountbatten Plan) partitioning the subcontinent into two dominions: India and Pakistan. Advanced the date of independence from June 1948 to August 15, 1947; oversaw Cyril Radcliffe's boundary demarcation and the tragic partition migration.

Book Note: Spectrum Chapter 25: Mountbatten Plan and Independence

text.headline: Decline of Mughals & Company Rule (1707–1857)
text.text: Decline of the Mughal Empire, rise of regional kingdoms, expansion of the British East India Company, and the Great Revolt of 1857.

text.headline: Direct Crown Rule & Early Nationalism (1858–1918)
text.text: Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858, modern English education, Indian National Congress (1885), Partition of Bengal (1905), and Swadeshi Movement.

text.headline: Gandhian Era & Road to Freedom (1919–1947)
text.text: Mass mobilization, Rowlatt Satyagraha, Non-Cooperation Movement, Civil Disobedience Movement, Quit India, and Independence.
